A peripherally-inserted central catheter (PICC) is a type of central venous catheter inserted through a peripheral vein, typically in the arm, and advanced to a central vein near the heart. 2. A peripheral arterial catheter (PAC) is a device inserted into an artery to monitor blood pressure or obtain blood samples. 3. Lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) are nations with lower levels of income and economic development, as defined by the World Bank. 4. A peripheral intravenous catheter (PIVC) is a small, flexible tube inserted into a peripheral vein to deliver medications or fluids. 5. Health and care workers (HCWs) are professionals involved in the delivery of healthcare services, including doctors, nurses, and allied health staff. 6. Intravenous (IV) therapy refers to the administration of fluids, medications, or nutrients directly into a vein. 7. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) is a scientific study design that randomly assigns participants to different groups to compare the effects of interventions. 8. A midline vascular catheter (MCV) is a type of catheter inserted into a peripheral vein, with the tip positioned in a larger vein, but not reaching the central veins. 9. Epidemiologist B.I. Mechnikov received training from the World Health Organization (WHO) on antimicrobial resistance in late 2022. Following this training, he contributed to implementing changes and establishing an infection control department at Mechnikov Hospital in Ukraine. 10. The WHO guidelines for preventing bloodstream infections and other infections associated with intravascular catheters emphasize the importance of monitoring and evaluating their impact. 11. Peripheral intravenous catheters (PIVCs) are among the most commonly used invasive medical devices worldwide. Complications related to their use should be routinely monitored, documented, and reported back to clinicians to enhance safety. 12. Monitoring, evaluation, and feedback are critical components of the WHO Multimodal Improvement Strategy (MMIS) for infection prevention and control (IPC). 13. WHO recommends a stepwise approach to implementing IPC interventions, starting with baseline assessments to evaluate impact and ensure sustainability. 14. Interventions to improve practices related to the use of PIVCs should include steps that focus on monitoring and feedback as essential elements. 15. Monitoring the impact of these guidelines involves several approaches: Assessing clinician education, training, and competencies in managing PIVCs, PICCs, and PACs, including insertion, maintenance, access, and removal. Evaluating adherence to recommended practices outlined in the guidelines. Identifying complications associated with PIVCs and PICCs and correlating these findings with adherence to clinical guidelines. Investigating all healthcare-associated bloodstream infections (BSIs) to determine their source and whether they are linked to intravascular catheters or other healthcare interventions. 16. Such monitoring allows clinicians to determine the proportion of BSIs that are catheter-associated, providing an indicator of the guidelines' effectiveness. 17. Ideally, data on catheter-associated infections should be correlated with valid measures of clinical activity, such as infections per 1,000 catheter days or per 1,000 inpatient bed days. 18. The WHO guidelines for preventing bloodstream infections and other catheter-associated infections are available as both printed documents and web-based resources. 20. These guidelines include all evidence presented to the Guideline Development Group (GDG) and will remain valid for five years. 21. The WHO Secretariat will monitor emerging scientific evidence and user needs to determine if updates to the recommendations are necessary during this period. 22. The Steering Group will continue to track research developments in preventing bloodstream infections and other catheter-associated infections, particularly in areas where evidence is limited or uncertain. 23. Following the publication and dissemination of the guidelines, any concerns about the validity of recommendations will be promptly communicated to implementers, and revisions will be made as needed. 24. The guidelines will be translated into Arabic, Chinese, French, Russian, and Spanish and disseminated through the WHO website, regional offices, and the Global Infection Prevention and Control Network (GIPCN). 25. Technical meetings will be held within WHO departments to share the guidelines with teams responsible for policy and program implementation. 26. Evidence briefs targeting policymakers and program managers will be developed to enhance the interpretation and uptake of the guidelines, especially in areas with limited technical expertise. 27. The recommendations will also be published as commentaries in peer-reviewed scientific journals to increase awareness. 28. Implementation tools reflecting WHO's multimodal strategies for IPC interventions will be developed in collaboration with regional offices, stakeholders, and field implementers. 29. WHO regional offices will be involved in adapting the guidelines to local contexts, including revising national guidelines or protocols as needed. 30. WHO departments and partners will support national and subnational groups in implementing the recommendations. 31. The WHO IPC team will collaborate with other departments to develop a research plan for effective implementation strategies. 32.
